questions.prompt: Which line runs a function when the chat form is submitted?
explanations: Correct: addEventListener waits for the event and then calls your function.
form.submit is a built-in method that sends the form; overwriting it doesn't listen for anything.

querySelector finds elements by selector; it doesn't take a function.

questions.prompt: How do you read what the visitor typed into <input id="chat-input">?
explanations: Correct: an input's current text is in its value property.
Inputs have no text property; use value.
An <input> has no inner HTML; what's typed lives in value.
Without the # it looks for a <chat-input> tag, not the id.
questions.hint: Inputs store what's typed in one property.

questions.prompt: Why should you show the visitor's message with textContent instead of innerHTML?
options: innerHTML would run any HTML the visitor types, which could inject code into your page
textContent is the only way to change text
explanations: Correct: that's cross-site scripting. textContent always shows text as plain text.
innerHTML can change text too; it's just unsafe for visitor input.
innerHTML works on almost any element.
textContent doesn't style anything.
questions.hint: What if someone types an tag?

questions.prompt: Which visitor message does /hello|hi/i.test(message) return true for?
explanations: Correct: the i flag ignores capitals, so HELLO matches hello.
None of the pattern's words appear in it.
"hey" is neither "hello" nor contains "hi".
"bye" contains neither.

Regex finds text; it doesn't style it.

questions.prompt: Which pattern matches an email address like ana.rao@uni.edu?
explanations: Correct: letters, @, letters, a real dot, letters.
A lone @ also matches "@ana", which isn't an email.
That matches the word "email", not an address.
\d is digits only, so letters wouldn't match.

questions.prompt: Your bot checks intents in order: greeting /\b(hi|hello)\b/i first, then skills /skill/i. What does it reply to "Hi, what are your skills?"
options: The greeting reply, because greeting is checked first
explanations: Correct: the first matching intent wins. Put specific intents (skills) before general ones (greeting).
Skills matches too, but it's checked after greeting has already won.
The loop returns at the first match, so there's only one reply.
Two intents match, so the fallback isn't used.

questions.prompt: What's a good fallback reply when no intent matches?
options: "Sorry, I didn't get that. Try asking about projects, skills or contact."
Repeat the visitor's message back to them
explanations: Correct: it admits the miss and tells visitors what they can ask.
Unhelpful: the visitor doesn't know what to try next.
Silence makes the chat look broken.
Echoing isn't an answer and doesn't help them.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order for handling one message.
options: Show the reply in the chat log
Find the first intent whose pattern matches
Prevent the form from reloading the page
explanations: Stop the reload, read what was typed, find the matching intent (or the fallback), then show the reply.
questions.hint: Start with what the browser does by default.

questions.prompt: Which CSS keeps the chat window in the bottom-right corner while the page scrolls?
explanations: Correct: fixed pins it to the window; bottom and right set the corner.
Float moves it to the right of its line, and it still scrolls away.
Relative only nudges it from its normal place in the page.
That aligns the text inside it, not the box itself.

questions.prompt: Spot the bug. The newest messages end up hidden below the bottom of the chat.
options: Change textContent to innerHTML on line 4
Use prepend instead of append on line 5
explanations: Correct: scroll the log to the bottom after adding each message.
Then the chat grows forever instead of scrolling.
That's unsafe and doesn't affect scrolling.
Newest-at-the-top works, but it breaks the usual chat order; scrolling is the expected fix.

questions.prompt: const m = "My name is Sam".match(/my name is (\w+)/i); What is m[1]?
explanations: Correct: m[1] is what the first capture group ( ) matched.

"my" is part of the pattern outside the group.
